episodes.title: Meet Sena and Daniel: What AI Can't Do for You
episodes.short_title: What AI Can't Do for You
episodes.summary: Sena, an Associate in Tokyo, asks her mentor Daniel, a People Manager in Seattle, what is left for humans as AI gets better. Using research from Harvard Business School and BCG, the World Economic Forum, Gallup, Microsoft, and a meta-analysis on leaders' emotional intelligence, they set out the show's three human skills, judgment, trust, and growth, and the thread that runs through them all: EQ.
episodes.practice: Listen to someone without interrupting, then ask: "What do you think?"
episodes.question: What's one thing you do at work that AI can't do for you, and how could you grow it?
sources: Dell'Acqua et al. (2023), Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, Harvard Business School Working Paper 24-013
World Economic Forum, Future of Jobs Report 2025
Gallup, research on managers and team engagement
Microsoft Work Trend Index 2025, The Year the Frontier Firm Is Born

Miao, Humphrey & Qian (2018), A cross-cultural meta-analysis of how leader emotional intelligence influences subordinate task performance and organizational citizenship behavior, Journal of World Business
Mattingly & Kraiger (2019), Can emotional intelligence be trained? A meta-analytical investigation, Human Resource Management Review

episodes.title: Interoceptive Awareness: The 30-Second Window
episodes.summary: A late-night message from a senior manager makes Sena's heart pound, and she almost sends a two-page apology. Daniel explains interoception, the sense that reads signals from inside your body, and why noticing them is the first EQ skill. They look at research on interoception and emotion, a study of traders on a London trading floor, and how naming a feeling can calm the brain's threat response. Then they turn it into a four-step habit: pause, scan, name, choose.
episodes.practice: Once a day, before replying to something that makes you react: pause, scan your body, name the feeling, then choose your next step. Write one sentence about it at night.
episodes.question: When did your body react before you knew what you were feeling, and what did it tell you?
sources: Critchley & Garfinkel (2017), Interoception and emotion, Current Opinion in Psychology
Kandasamy et al. (2016), Interoceptive Ability Predicts Survival on a London Trading Floor, Scientific Reports
Lieberman et al. (2007), Putting Feelings Into Words: Affect Labeling Disrupts Amygdala Activity in Response to Affective Stimuli, Psychological Science
Gross (1998), Antecedent- and response-focused emotion regulation, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Damasio, the somatic marker hypothesis
episodes.title_ja: 内受容感覚：30秒の窓
episodes.summary_ja: 夜11時、シニアマネージャーからのメッセージで心臓がドキドキし、セナは2ページの謝罪を送りかけます。ダニエルが、体の内側のサインを読む感覚「内受容感覚」と、それに気づくことが最初のEQスキルである理由を説明。ロンドンのトレーダーの研究や、気持ちに名前をつけると脳の脅威反応が落ち着く研究を紹介し、「止まる・探る・名前をつける・選ぶ」の4ステップにまとめます。
episodes.hook_ja:
夜11時、上司からのメッセージに心臓がドキッ。すぐ長文で返したくなったこと、ありませんか？
返信する前の「30秒」で、気持ちに振り回されなくなる方法を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 体の内側のサインを読む力「内受容感覚」とは
ロンドンのトレーダーの研究（小規模で、因果関係までは言えない点も）
気持ちに名前をつけると、脳の脅威反応が落ち着くという研究
止まる・探る・名前をつける・選ぶ、の4ステップ
phrases: Can we talk about the numbers in your deck? Something looks off.
資料の数字について話せる？何かおかしく見えるんだ。
This is anxiety. My heart is pounding because I'm worried I made a mistake.
これは不安だ。ミスをしたかもしれないと心配で、心臓がドキドキしている。
What do I actually know, and what's the smallest helpful next step?
実際に何がわかっている？一番小さくて役に立つ次の一歩は？
episodes.practice_ja: 反応してしまう場面で、返事をする前に「止まる・体を探る・気持ちに名前をつける・次の一歩を選ぶ」。夜に1文だけ書き留める。
episodes.yt_title: Your Body Knows You're Upset Before You Do

episodes.title: Ownership: Acting Like It's Yours
episodes.summary: A half-finished FAQ that nobody asked Sena to write comes up in a team meeting, and her face gets hot. Daniel explains psychological ownership, the feeling that something is "mine" even when you don't legally own it, and a lab study showing that simply making a when, where, and how plan can quiet the pull of unfinished tasks. He shares the two-minute fix he once left for "someone," and they compare how ownership looks in Japanese and US workplaces. Then they connect it to self-management: finish it, hand it off, or drop it out loud.
episodes.practice: Close one unfinished loose end that nobody asked you to close: finish it, hand it off, or drop it out loud, and if you can't do it now, write a when, where, and how plan.
episodes.question: What's one half-finished thing you could close today: finish it, hand it off, or stop it out loud?
sources: Masicampo & Baumeister (2011), Consider It Done! Plan Making Can Eliminate the Cognitive Effects of Unfulfilled Goals, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Pierce, Kostova & Dirks (2001), Toward a Theory of Psychological Ownership in Organizations, Academy of Management Review

Van Dyne & Pierce (2004), Psychological Ownership and Feelings of Possession: Three Field Studies Predicting Employee Attitudes and Organizational Citizenship Behavior, Journal of Organizational Behavior
episodes.title_ja: オーナーシップ：自分ごととして動く
episodes.summary_ja: 誰にも頼まれずに書き始めたFAQが半分で止まっていて、会議でそれが話題になり、セナの顔が熱くなります。ダニエルが、法的に持っていなくても「自分のもの」と感じる心理的オーナーシップと、「いつ・どこで・どうやるか」の計画を立てるだけで未完了の仕事が頭を占めなくなる研究を紹介。日米の職場でのオーナーシップの違いを比べ、自己管理の「仕上げる・引き継ぐ・声に出してやめる」につなげます。
episodes.hook_ja:
自分から始めたのに、途中で止まっている仕事。会議で話題に出て、顔が熱くなったことは？
「やりかけ」を気持ちよく閉じる、オーナーシップの育て方を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 持ち主じゃなくても「自分ごと」と感じる、心理的オーナーシップ
「いつ・どこで・どうやるか」を書くだけで頭が軽くなる研究
日本とアメリカ、オーナーシップの見せ方の違い
仕上げる・引き継ぐ・声に出してやめる、の3択
phrases: I noticed this link is broken. Do you mind if I fix it?
このリンクが切れているのに気づきました。直してもいいですか？
The partner FAQ is done. Here's the link.
パートナー向けFAQが完成しました。リンクはこちらです。

episodes.title: Naming Emotions: Beyond 'Fine'
episodes.summary: When a project she wanted goes to someone else, Sena tells her manager she's fine, but all afternoon something feels heavy. Daniel helps her look past "fine" and "stressed" to find what's really there: disappointed, embarrassed, and a little relieved. They explore emotional granularity, the skill of naming feelings precisely, through a diary study by Lisa Feldman Barrett and colleagues, a large smartphone study on coping, and an experiment where naming fear changed people's body reactions to a spider. Sena brings in the Japanese word daijoubu, and Daniel shares how calling loneliness "stress" cost him three months.
episodes.practice: Three times a day, name your current emotion as precisely as you can; if the first word is fine, good, bad, or stressed, find two more specific options and pick the closest.
episodes.question: How do you really feel about your work today? Try a word more exact than "fine."
sources: Barrett, Gross, Christensen & Benvenuto (2001), Knowing what you're feeling and knowing what to do about it: Mapping the relation between emotion differentiation and emotion regulation, Cognition and Emotion

Kalokerinos, Erbas, Ceulemans & Kuppens (2019), Differentiate to Regulate: Low Negative Emotion Differentiation Is Associated With Ineffective Use but Not Selection of Emotion-Regulation Strategies, Psychological Science
Kashdan, Barrett & McKnight (2015), Unpacking Emotion Differentiation: Transforming Unpleasant Experience by Perceiving Distinctions in Negativity, Current Directions in Psychological Science
Kircanski, Lieberman & Craske (2012), Feelings Into Words: Contributions of Language to Exposure Therapy, Psychological Science
episodes.title_ja: 感情に名前をつける：「大丈夫」の先へ
episodes.summary_ja: 準備していたプロジェクトが別の人に決まり、セナは「大丈夫です」と答えますが、午後ずっと気持ちが重いまま。ダニエルと一緒に「大丈夫」「ストレス」の下にある、がっかり・恥ずかしい・少しほっとした気持ちを見つけます。気持ちを細かく言い分ける「感情の粒度」について、リサ・フェルドマン・バレットらの日記研究、スマホを使った大規模研究、クモへの恐怖の実験を紹介。日本語の「大丈夫」の使い方も話します。
episodes.hook_ja:
本当はモヤモヤしているのに、つい「大丈夫です」と言ってしまう…そんなこと、ありませんか？
「大丈夫」の下にある本当の気持ちに名前をつける方法を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 気持ちを細かく言い分ける力「感情の粒度」
リサ・フェルドマン・バレットらの日記研究と、スマホを使った大規模研究
気持ちを言葉にするとクモへの恐怖が和らいだ実験
日本語の「大丈夫」は、なぜ便利で、なぜ危ないのか
phrases: I was looking forward to that project. Could we talk about what I could lead next?
あのプロジェクトを楽しみにしていました。次に私がリードできることについて話せますか？
What exactly are you missing right now?
今、具体的に何が足りないと思う？
I feel relieved, but a little guilty.
ほっとしたけど、ちょっと罪悪感もある。
episodes.practice_ja: 1日3回、今の気持ちをできるだけ正確に名前にする。「大丈夫・良い・悪い・ストレス」なら、もっと具体的な言葉を2つ探して近いほうを選ぶ。

episodes.title: Asking for Feedback (and Using It)
episodes.summary: A colleague in New York tells Sena she could push back more in meetings, and Sena answers with a long explanation that quietly closes the door. Daniel shares research on feedback seeking, including a study of 387 managers and their bosses, peers, and direct reports, a meta-analysis showing that over a third of feedback interventions made performance worse, and why asking alone is not enough. He also tells the story of the retrospective where he asked his team for feedback and then argued with it. Together they practice a self-management skill: ask for one thing, and answer with only "Thank you."
episodes.practice: Ask one person, "What's one thing I could do better?" and respond only with "Thank you," with no defending and no explaining.
episodes.question: Who could you ask "What's one thing I could do better?" this week, and how will you answer?
sources: Ashford & Cummings (1983), Feedback as an Individual Resource: Personal Strategies of Creating Information, Organizational Behavior and Human Performance
Ashford & Tsui (1991), Self-Regulation for Managerial Effectiveness: The Role of Active Feedback Seeking, Academy of Management Journal
Kluger & DeNisi (1996), The Effects of Feedback Interventions on Performance: A Historical Review, a Meta-Analysis, and a Preliminary Feedback Intervention Theory, Psychological Bulletin
Ashford, Blatt & VandeWalle (2003), Reflections on the Looking Glass: A Review of Research on Feedback-Seeking Behavior in Organizations, Journal of Management
Anseel, Beatty, Shen, Lievens & Sackett (2015), How Are We Doing After 30 Years? A Meta-Analytic Review of the Antecedents and Outcomes of Feedback-Seeking Behavior, Journal of Management
Stone & Heen (2014), Thanks for the Feedback: The Science and Art of Receiving Feedback Well, book
episodes.title_ja: フィードバックを求めて、生かす
episodes.summary_ja: ニューヨークの同僚から「会議でもっと意見を言っていい」と言われたセナは、長い説明で返してしまい、相手は「気にしないで！」とドアを閉じてしまいます。387人のマネージャーの研究、フィードバックの3分の1以上がかえって成果を下げたメタ分析、聞くだけでは足りない理由を紹介。ダニエルが振り返りで反論してしまった失敗談も。自己管理のスキルとして「1つだけ聞いて、ありがとうだけ言う」を練習します。
episodes.hook_ja:
フィードバックをもらった瞬間、つい説明や言い訳を始めてしまうこと、ありませんか？
相手がまた本音をくれるようになる「受け取り方」を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 387人のマネージャーの研究
フィードバックの3分の1以上が、かえって成果を下げたメタ分析
振り返りで反論してしまった、ダニエルの失敗
「1つだけ聞いて、ありがとうだけ言う」練習
phrases: What's one thing I could do better?
私がもっと良くできることを1つ挙げるとしたら？

こう言ってくれましたよね。それを試してみました。違いに気づきましたか？

episodes.title: Making Your 1:1 Count
episodes.summary: Sena's 1:1 with her manager in Tokyo has become a status report, and when it gets canceled she feels relieved. Daniel shares research by Steven Rogelberg and colleagues on one-on-one meetings, along with Gallup findings on managers, meaningful feedback, and engagement, plus the story of a quiet engineer he lost because their 1:1s were always his meeting. They compare how 1:1s work in Japan and the US and introduce the fourth EQ domain, relationship management. The practice: bring one question and one kinkyou, a short update about yourself, to your next 1:1.
episodes.practice: Bring one question you really want answered and one short personal or work update (kinkyou) to your next 1:1, share them near the start, and afterward write one sentence about how the other person reacted.
episodes.question: What's one real question you want to ask in your next one-on-one?
sources: Flinchum, Kreamer, Rogelberg & Gooty (2023, online 2022), One-on-one meetings between managers and direct reports: A new opportunity for meeting science, Organizational Psychology Review
Rogelberg (2022), Make the Most of Your One-on-One Meetings, Harvard Business Review
Rogelberg (2024), Glad We Met: The Art and Science of 1:1 Meetings, book
Gallup (2023, updated 2026), A Great Manager's Most Important Habit, Gallup Workplace
Gallup, How to Improve Employee Engagement in the Workplace, Gallup Workplace

1on1がただの進捗報告になって、キャンセルされるとちょっとホッとする…そんなこと、ありませんか？

points_ja: スティーブン・ロゲルバーグらの1on1の研究
マネージャーとエンゲージメントについてのギャラップの調査

episodes.hook:

episodes.title: Say It Clearly: Low-Context Communication
episodes.summary: Sena's polite, carefully explained email to a product manager in Seattle hid its one question in the last paragraph, and the decision never came. Daniel shares research by Boaz Keysar and Anne Henly on how speakers overestimate how well they are understood, and by Justin Kruger, Nicholas Epley and colleagues on how tone gets lost in email, plus the story of a one-line message he sent to an engineer in Tokyo. They compare high-context and low-context communication in Japan and the US and explore the social awareness skill of reading your message from the other person's screen. The practice: rewrite one message as conclusion, request with a date, then details.
episodes.practice: Pick one message you need to send and rewrite it in this order: the conclusion or decision first, then what you need from the reader and by when, then the details. Add one true line of warmth, and before sending, ask: if I only read the first two lines, would I know what to do?
episodes.question: Take one message you need to send today. What's your first line: the conclusion and what you need?
sources: Keysar & Henly (2002), Speakers' Overestimation of Their Effectiveness, Psychological Science
Kruger, Epley, Parker & Ng (2005), Egocentrism Over E-Mail: Can We Communicate as Well as We Think?, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Meyer (2014), The Culture Map: Breaking Through the Invisible Boundaries of Global Business, PublicAffairs
Hall (1976), Beyond Culture, book
episodes.title_ja: はっきり伝える：ローコンテクストなコミュニケーション

episodes.hook_ja:
丁寧に書いたメールなのに、一番大事な質問への返事が来ない…そんな経験、ありませんか？
最初の2行で伝わる「ローコンテクスト」な書き方を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 話し手は自分が思うほど伝わっていない（ケイサーとヘンリーの研究）
メールではトーンが伝わりにくい（クルーガーとエプリーらの研究）
1行メッセージで東京のエンジニアを困らせた、ダニエルの失敗

マークさん、レポートについて急ぎで決めていただきたいことがあります。

火曜日までに教えてもらえますか？

最初の2行だけ読んで、何をすればいいかわかる？

episodes.yt_title: Why Your Emails Aren't as Clear as You Think
episodes.hook:

episodes.title: Earning Trust with Peers

Daniel shares Ayelet Gneezy and Nicholas Epley's research showing that keeping a promise matters but going beyond it adds little, along with Schweitzer, Hershey and Bradlow's study of how consistent actions rebuild trust while deception leaves lasting damage, and the Mayer, Davis and Schoorman model of ability, benevolence and integrity. episodes.title: Influence Without Authority
episodes.summary: Sena needs one small change from a data team in Seattle, but her ticket and polite reminders keep getting pushed to 'later,' and she is tempted to escalate. Daniel shares Francis Flynn and Vanessa Lake's research showing people underestimate how often others will say yes to a direct request, Gary Yukl and Bruce Tracey's field study on which influence tactics build real commitment with peers, and Allan Cohen and David Bradford's idea of 'currencies,' plus the story of the escalation that cost him a year of goodwill. The practice: before asking another team for something, first ask them what they need.

Listen without jumping to your request, then write down two or three things you learned about their world.

episodes.title: Speaking Up When You Disagree
episodes.summary: In a team meeting, everyone nods at a plan to launch a new dashboard to all regions at once, and Sena stays quiet even though she knows some regions have missing data. Daniel shares Frances Milliken, Elizabeth Morrison, and Patricia Hewlin's interview study, in which 85 percent of employees said they had felt unable to raise an important issue with their boss, and Charlan Nemeth's research showing that authentic dissent helps groups find more and better solutions than a role-played devil's advocate. He tells the story of the launch review where his silence made a colleague silent too. They compare Japan's kuuki wo yomu, reading the air, with the US idea of disagree and commit, and treat speaking up as self-management: noticing the fear, and choosing to say it anyway. The practice: agree, concern, question.
episodes.practice: When you disagree with something in a meeting, say it once, in one sentence: start with what you agree with, share your concern as information, and end with a question, like "I see it a little differently. Here's one concern. What do you think?" If you can't say it in the room, tell the person who decides within 24 hours. Afterward, write down what you were afraid would happen, and what actually happened.
episodes.question: When did you last stay quiet in a meeting? What one sentence could you have said?
sources: Milliken, Morrison & Hewlin (2003), An Exploratory Study of Employee Silence: Issues that Employees Don't Communicate Upward and Why, Journal of Management Studies
Nemeth, Brown & Rogers (2001), Devil's advocate versus authentic dissent: stimulating quantity and quality, European Journal of Social Psychology

episodes.title: What Changes When You Lead
episodes.summary: After her manager cancels their one-on-one for the third time and she sees his calendar packed from nine to seven, Sena realizes she doesn't really know what a manager's job is, even though leading is her goal. Today's challenge: ask your manager what surprised them most when they became a manager, and just listen.
episodes.practice: Today, ask your manager one question: "What surprised you most when you became a manager?" Ask it in a one-on-one, after a meeting, or in a short message. Then just listen, without advice. Afterward, write down one thing that changes how you see their job.

episodes.title: Giving Feedback with SBI
episodes.summary: The dashboard launches with zero wrong numbers because Ryo came in at seven to run his data check, but Sena's thank-you is just "great job!" and gets a thumbs-up back. Daniel shares Erica Boothby and Vanessa Bohns's research showing that people underestimate how good their compliments make others feel, and John Hattie and Helen Timperley's review finding that praise about the person teaches little compared with feedback about the task and process. episodes.summary_ja: 4日連続で朝早く来て疲れた様子のリョウさん。担当分は3日遅れていて、セナはやわらかすぎるメッセージを書いては消しています。正直な会話は思っているより良い結果になるという研究と、よく聞いてもらうと人は不安が下がり身構えにくくなるという研究を紹介。ダニエルが冗談でごまかし続けた6週間の話も。日本の「察し」「本音と建前」とアメリカのフィードバック・サンドイッチを比べ、第1シーズンを振り返ります。

言いにくいことを、関係を壊さずに伝える方法を英語で学ぶ、シーズン1最終回🎧（日本語字幕あり）

よく聞いてもらうと、人は身構えにくくなるという研究
冗談でごまかし続けた6週間、ダニエルの失敗
「察し」「本音と建前」とフィードバック・サンドイッチ、そしてシーズン1の振り返り
episodes.practice_ja: 伝えたいことを、仕事とその影響についての1文で書く。言う前に「本当のところ、元気？」と聞いて、相手が話し終わるまで聞く。

episodes.hook:
You know you need to say it. So you write a soft message, delete it, and write it again.
Learn how to say the hard thing kindly, without breaking the relationship. Season 1 finale.

Why people get less defensive when they feel heard

episodes.title: When You Make a Mistake
episodes.summary: At eleven at night, Sena finds that the region two numbers she sent Mark counted one day twice, just before they go into Laura's deck, and two voices fight in her head: fix it quietly, or call herself careless. Daniel shares Kenneth Savitsky, Nicholas Epley, and Thomas Gilovich's studies showing that people expect to be judged much more harshly for their mistakes than they really are, and Nina Keith and Michael Frese's meta-analysis showing that learning from errors helps most on new problems. He tells the story of the "version two" he sent without saying what changed, and they compare shimatsusho and hou-ren-sou in Japan with "own it, fix it, move on" in the US. Today's challenge: report one mistake in three sentences: the fact, the impact, and the next step.
episodes.practice: Today, report one mistake, big or small, in three sentences: the fact, the impact, and the next step.
sources: Savitsky, Epley & Gilovich (2001), Do Others Judge Us as Harshly as We Think? Overestimating the Impact of Our Failures, Shortcomings, and Mishaps, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Keith & Frese (2008), Effectiveness of Error Management Training: A Meta-Analysis, Journal of Applied Psychology
episodes.yt_title: How to Report a Mistake at Work (Without Panicking)
episodes.hook:
You find an error in numbers you already sent, and a voice says: just fix it quietly.
Learn three sentences that report any mistake clearly and keep people's trust.
points: Why we expect much harsher judgment than we get (Savitsky, Epley & Gilovich)
Errors as information: a meta-analysis of error management training
The "version two" that cost Daniel six months of trust
Shimatsusho and hou-ren-sou vs "own it, fix it, move on"
episodes.title_ja: ミスをしたとき、最初の1時間
episodes.hook_ja:
送ったあとの数字にミスを発見。「こっそり直せばバレないかも」…そんな声が聞こえたこと、ありませんか？
事実・影響・次の一手、3つの文で信頼を失わずにミスを報告する方法を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 人は、他人が思うよりずっと厳しく自分を評価している
ミスが一番役に立つのは「次の問題が違うとき」
こっそり直した「バージョン2」で半年の信頼を失った話
始末書・ホウレンソウと「Own it, fix it, move on」
episodes.summary_ja: 夜11時、マークさんに送ったリージョン2の数字で1日分が二重に数えられていたことに気づいたセナ。「こっそり直せばいい」という声と「なんて不注意なの」という声がぶつかります。ミスをした人は実際よりずっと厳しく評価されると思い込むという研究と、ミスから学ぶ研修は新しい課題で特に効くというメタ分析を紹介。何が変わったかを言わずに「バージョン2」を送ったダニエルの失敗談、日本の始末書やホウレンソウとアメリカの「Own it, fix it, move on」の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 大きくても小さくても、ミスを1つ、今日のうちに「事実・影響・次の一手」の3つの文で報告する。

episodes.title: Stress Is a Signal
episodes.summary: The day before a call with Laura, Sena notices her jaw is clenched in the office elevator, but tells Ryo, "I'm fine, just a little busy." Daniel shares Alia Crum, Peter Salovey, and Shawn Achor's study, where employees who watched short videos about stress being enhancing reported fewer symptoms and better performance, and Bosshard and Gomez's 2024 meta-analysis showing that such interventions help only a little. He tells the story of the jaw his wife noticed before he did, and the sharp words over a typo, and they compare gaman and daijoubu in Japan with "I'm slammed" in the US. Today's challenge: the moment you feel stress today, write down one body signal.
episodes.practice: Today, the moment you feel stress, write down one body signal: where it is, what it feels like, and what time it is.
sources: Crum, Salovey & Achor (2013), Rethinking Stress: The Role of Mindsets in Determining the Stress Response, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

Bosshard & Gomez (2024), Effectiveness of stress arousal reappraisal and stress-is-enhancing mindset interventions on task performance outcomes: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Scientific Reports
episodes.yt_title: Stress at Work Is a Signal: How to Read It
episodes.hook:
Your jaw is tight, you haven't breathed out, and you still say "I'm fine, just busy."
Learn to catch one body signal and turn it into a plan, with honest research on stress.
points: Stress mindsets: a study of 388 employees during layoffs (Crum, Salovey & Achor)
A 2024 meta-analysis of 35 trials: helpful, but small
The clenched jaw Daniel's wife noticed first
Gaman and "daijoubu" vs "I'm slammed"
episodes.title_ja: ストレスは体からのサイン
episodes.hook_ja:
あごに力が入って、息も止まっている。それでも「大丈夫、ちょっと忙しいだけ」って言っていませんか？
ストレスのサインを1つつかまえて、次の行動に変える方法を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 人員削減中の388人、9分の動画で変わったこと
35の実験をまとめたら「効果は小さい」という正直な結果
ダニエルより先に妻が気づいた「食いしばり」
我慢と「大丈夫」、アメリカの「I'm slammed」
episodes.summary_ja: ローラさんとの通話の前日、エレベーターであごを食いしばっていることに気づいたセナ。それでもリョウさんには「大丈夫、忙しいだけ」と答えます。ストレスは役に立つこともあると伝える短い動画を見た社員が症状の減少を報告した研究と、こうした介入の効果は小さいという2024年のメタ分析を紹介。妻に食いしばりを指摘され、打ち間違いでチームに強く当たってしまったダニエルの失敗談、日本の我慢とアメリカの「I'm slammed」の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日ストレスを感じたその瞬間に、体のサインを1つ書き留める（どこに、どんな感じで、何時か）。

episodes.title: Nerves Before You Speak
episodes.summary: The night before she explains her fix to a director in English, Sena practices alone in a small meeting room, and every "calm down" makes her heart beat faster. Daniel shares Alison Wood Brooks's experiments, where saying "I am excited" helped people sing, speak, and solve math better than trying to stay calm, and Ethan Kross's research on coaching yourself by name, with honest limits. He tells the story of the review his VP called "a weather report," and they compare "kinchou shite imasu ga" in Japan with "I'm excited to be here" in the US. Today's challenge: before you speak today, say "I'm excited" instead of "calm down," then say your first sentence.
episodes.practice: Before you speak today, in a meeting, on a call, or with a quick question, don't tell yourself to calm down. Say "I'm excited," out loud or quietly, and then say your first sentence.
sources: Brooks (2014), Get Excited: Reappraising Pre-Performance Anxiety as Excitement, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General
Kross, Bruehlman-Senecal, Park, Burson, Dougherty, Shablack, Bremner, Moser & Ayduk (2014), Self-Talk as a Regulatory Mechanism: How You Do It Matters, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology

Bosshard & Gomez (2024), Effectiveness of stress arousal reappraisal and stress-is-enhancing mindset interventions on task performance outcomes: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, Scientific Reports
episodes.yt_title: Nervous Before a Presentation? Don't Say "Calm Down"
episodes.hook:
Five minutes before you speak, your heart is racing, and "calm down" only makes it faster.
Learn one sentence for the last five minutes before a meeting, backed by honest research on nerves.
points: "I am excited" vs "I am calm": Brooks's karaoke, speech, and math experiments
Coaching yourself by name: 7 studies by Kross and colleagues
The review Daniel's VP called "a weather report"
"Kinchou shite imasu ga" vs "I'm excited to be here"
episodes.title_ja: 話す前の緊張には「落ち着いて」より「ワクワクしてる」
episodes.hook_ja:
明日は英語で5分の説明。「落ち着いて」と自分に言うほど、心臓が速くなる…そんな経験ありませんか？
話す直前の5分間に効く「ひとこと」を、研究とセナの本番前夜から英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: カラオケの正確さが約81%に上がった「ひとこと」
自分を名前で呼ぶと、スピーチの評価が上がった
VPに「天気予報みたい」と言われたダニエルの発表
日本の「緊張していますが」とアメリカの「I'm excited」
episodes.summary_ja: 英語でディレクターに説明する前夜、小さな会議室で一人練習するセナ。「落ち着いて」と言うほど心臓は速くなります。「ワクワクしている」と言うと、歌・スピーチ・数学の成績が上がったブルックスの実験と、自分を名前で励ますクロスらの研究を、限界も含めて紹介。VPに「天気予報みたい」と言われたダニエルの失敗談、日本の「緊張していますが」とアメリカの「I'm excited to be here」の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日話す前に「落ち着いて」ではなく「ワクワクしている」と（声に出しても心の中でも）言い、それから最初の一文を話す。

episodes.title: Anger Without Damage
episodes.summary: Right after a call that went well, a colleague from another team publicly calls Sena's work "duplicate," and her finger hovers over the Enter key with an angry reply. Daniel shares Brad Bushman's study, where venting on a punching bag made angry people more aggressive than sitting quietly, and a 2024 meta-analysis of 154 studies showing that lowering arousal reduces anger. He tells the story of a reply-all email he sent at 11:04 p.m., and they compare quiet anger in Japan, like a cold "kashikomarimashita," with "let's take this offline" in the US. Today's challenge: if a message makes you angry today, write a draft, wait twenty minutes, and read it again before you send it.
episodes.practice: If a message makes you angry today, don't reply right away. Write your answer as a draft, step away for twenty minutes, and read it again before you send it.
sources: Bushman (2002), Does Venting Anger Feed or Extinguish the Flame? Catharsis, Rumination, Distraction, Anger, and Aggressive Responding, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
Kjærvik & Bushman (2024), A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage?, Clinical Psychology Review
episodes.yt_title: Angry at Work? What to Do Before You Hit Send
episodes.hook:
A colleague criticizes your work in a public channel, and your angry reply is ready to send.
Learn what to do in the twenty minutes after anger, so you can answer without damage.
points: Does venting help? Bushman's punching bag study with 600 students
A 2024 meta-analysis of 154 studies: lowering arousal reduces anger
Daniel's reply-all email at 11:04 p.m., and six months of repair
Quiet anger in Japan vs "let's take this offline" in the US
episodes.title_ja: 仕事の怒りに、ダメージを残さない方法
episodes.hook_ja:
みんなが見ているチャンネルで、自分の仕事を「重複作業」と言われた。怒りの返信、送信ボタンの上で指が止まっていませんか？
怒ったあとの20分で何をするか、ダメージを残さない返し方を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: サンドバッグで発散すると、怒りは増えた？
154の研究が示す、怒りを下げる体の使い方
夜11時4分の返信メール、ダニエルの6か月の代償
冷たい「かしこまりました」とアメリカの「offline」
episodes.summary_ja: 会議がうまくいった直後、他チームの人に公開チャンネルで仕事を「重複作業」と書かれたセナ。怒りの返信を送る寸前でダニエルに連絡します。サンドバッグで発散したグループのほうが攻撃的になったブッシュマンの研究と、体の高ぶりを下げると怒りが減るという154研究のメタ分析を紹介。夜11時4分に全員返信を送ったダニエルの失敗談、日本の静かな怒りとアメリカの「Let's take this offline」の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日メッセージにイラッとしたら、すぐに返信せず下書きに書き、20分離れてから読み返して送る。

episodes.title: Disappointment and Bouncing Back
episodes.summary: Laura decides to move region three to the standard table, and Sena's almost-finished dashboard is stopped after three weeks of work. Daniel shares Eskreis-Winkler and Fishbach's finding that people learn less from their own failures because they tune out, and a meta-analysis by Tannenbaum and Cerasoli showing that structured debriefs improved performance by about 20 to 25 percent. He tells the story of a four-month proposal that was rejected and the three weeks he disappeared, and they compare "shikata ga nai" and "hansei" in Japan with "lessons learned" and "disagree and commit" in the US. Today's challenge: pick one thing that didn't go the way you hoped and write down one lesson you'll use next time.
episodes.practice: Pick one thing that didn't go the way you hoped, today or recently, and write down one lesson from it: not what went wrong, but one thing you'll do differently next time.
sources: Eskreis-Winkler & Fishbach (2019), Not Learning From Failure—the Greatest Failure of All, Psychological Science
Tannenbaum & Cerasoli (2013), Do Team and Individual Debriefs Enhance Performance? A Meta-Analysis, Human Factors
episodes.yt_title: Your Project Got Cancelled? How to Bounce Back at Work
episodes.hook:
Three weeks of work, almost finished, and then: "So we stop it. Today."
Learn four steps for the day after a disappointment, and one question that turns it into a lesson.
points: Why we learn less from our own failures (Eskreis-Winkler & Fishbach, 1,600+ people)
Debriefs improved performance by about 20–25% across 46 samples
Daniel's rejected four-month proposal, and the three weeks he disappeared
"Shikata ga nai" and "hansei" in Japan vs "disagree and commit" in the US
episodes.title_ja: がんばった仕事が止まった日、立ち直るための4ステップ
episodes.hook_ja:
3週間かけて、ほぼ完成。なのに「今日で止める」。がんばった仕事がなくなった日、心がずしんと重くなったことはありませんか？
失望を「次に活きる学び」に変える4つのステップを、英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 人は自分の失敗から学びにくい？1,600人の実験
ふり返り(デブリーフ)で成果が約2割アップ
4か月の提案が却下、ダニエルが消えた3週間
「仕方がない」と「disagree and commit」
episodes.summary_ja: ローラさんの決定で、ほぼ完成していた地域3のダッシュボードが止まったセナ。人は自分の失敗から目をそらして学びにくいというエスクライス＝ウィンクラーとフィッシュバックの研究と、ふり返り(デブリーフ)で成果が約20〜25％上がったというタネンバウムとセラソリのメタ分析を紹介します。4か月かけた提案が却下されて「消えた」ダニエルの失敗談、日本の「仕方がない」「反省」とアメリカの「disagree and commit」の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日でも最近でも、思いどおりにいかなかったことを1つ選び、「次は違うやり方をすること」を1つ書き出す。

episodes.title: Envy as Information
episodes.summary: A colleague who joined the company the same year as Sena is chosen for three months of launch planning in Seattle, and Sena can't stop feeling a heavy stone in her stomach. Daniel explains benign and malicious envy with research by van de Ven, Zeelenberg and Pieters, where benign envy motivated people more than admiration, and a study by Lange and Crusius of 370 runners, where benign envy went with higher race goals. He tells the story of the time envy made him question a peer's slides in public, and they compare same-year "dōki" comparisons in Japan with open ambition in the US. Today's challenge: if you feel envy today, write one sentence that starts with "I want" and name the thing, not the person.
episodes.practice: If you feel envy today, toward a colleague, a friend, or even a post online, write one sentence that starts with "I want." Name the thing, not the person.
sources: van de Ven, Zeelenberg & Pieters (2011), Why Envy Outperforms Admiration, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
Lange & Crusius (2015), Dispositional Envy Revisited: Unraveling the Motivational Dynamics of Benign and Malicious Envy, Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
episodes.yt_title: Jealous of a Coworker? What Envy Tells You About Your Goals
episodes.hook:
A colleague who started the same year as you gets the opportunity you wanted, and you can't even type "Congratulations."
Learn how to turn envy into one clear sentence about what you want, and one small step.
points: Benign vs malicious envy, and why benign envy can outperform admiration
370 marathon runners: benign envy went with higher goals
Daniel's envy of a peer's conference talk, and the question that changed it
Same-year "dōki" comparison in Japan vs open ambition in the US
episodes.title_ja: 同期がうらやましい。その気持ちが教えてくれること
episodes.hook_ja:
同期の抜てきのニュース。「おめでとう」を打っては消して、また消して。そんな自分がいやになったことはありませんか？
うらやましさを「本当に欲しいもの」の一文に変える方法を、英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 良い妬みは、憧れより人を動かす？
マラソンランナー370人と「目標」の関係
ダニエルが同僚のスライドにした、後悔の質問
日本の「同期」比べとアメリカの堂々とした野心
episodes.summary_ja: 同期のミサキさんが3か月シアトルのローンチ計画に抜てきされ、おなかに重い石を感じるセナ。良性の妬みは憧れよりもやる気を生むというファン・デ・フェンらの研究と、良性の妬みが強いランナーほど高い目標を立てていたというランゲとクルジウスの研究を紹介します。同僚の講演をうらやんで会議で水を差したダニエルの失敗談、日本の「同期」比べとアメリカのオープンな野心の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日うらやましいと感じたら、「私は〜したい」で始まる一文を書く。人ではなく、欲しい「もの」に名前をつける。

episodes.title: Impostor Feelings
episodes.summary: Days before presenting her pipeline to Mark's team in Seattle, Sena types "Basically a faster spreadsheet" under the title of her first slide, and a small voice says everyone will find out. Daniel shares a systematic review by Bravata and colleagues of 62 studies, where impostor feelings ranged from 9% to 82% depending on how they were measured, and Basima Tewfik's research, where people with workplace impostor thoughts were rated as better with others but had lower self-esteem. He tells the story of underselling himself to his VP and the "Receipts" file he has kept ever since, and they compare Japanese modesty, which listeners quietly add back, with US meetings, where small words are taken literally. Today's challenge: write down three pieces of evidence of your own work: a number, a result, or something someone said to you.
episodes.practice: Write down three pieces of evidence of your own work. Facts, not feelings: a number, a result, or something someone said to you.
sources: Bravata, Watts, Keefer, Madhusudhan, Taylor, Clark, Nelson, Cokley & Hagg (2020), Prevalence, Predictors, and Treatment of Impostor Syndrome: a Systematic Review, Journal of General Internal Medicine
Tewfik (2022), The Impostor Phenomenon Revisited: Examining the Relationship between Workplace Impostor Thoughts and Interpersonal Effectiveness at Work, Academy of Management Journal
Clance & Imes (1978), The Imposter Phenomenon in High Achieving Women: Dynamics and Therapeutic Intervention, Psychotherapy: Theory, Research & Practice
episodes.yt_title: Feel Like an Impostor at Work? Answer the Voice With Evidence
episodes.hook:
You finally get the chance you wanted, and a small voice says, "They'll find out you're not that good."
Learn how to answer impostor thoughts with three pieces of evidence and one sentence that owns your work.
points: 62 studies: impostor feelings ranged from 9% to 82%, depending on how they were measured
Why people with impostor thoughts were rated better with others, and what it costs them
Daniel undersold himself to his VP, and started a "Receipts" file
Japanese modesty vs US meetings, where small words are taken literally
episodes.title_ja: 「いつかバレる」と思ったら。自分の成果に証拠で答える
episodes.hook_ja:
初めての大きな発表。スライドに「要するに、ただの表計算です」と小さく書き足してしまう…そんな経験はありませんか？
「自分なんて」の声に、3つの証拠で言い返す方法を英語で身につけよう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 62の研究でわかった「9〜82%」という幅の正体
インポスター思考がある人ほど、人づき合いは高評価？
ダニエルがVPの前で自分を小さく見せた日
「つまらないものですが」が通じない会議
episodes.summary_ja: マークさんのチームへの発表を前に、スライドに「要するに、速くなったスプレッドシート」と書いてしまうセナ。62の研究をまとめたブラバタらのレビュー（割合は測り方次第で9〜82%）と、インポスター思考のある人ほど対人面で高く評価されたが自尊心は低かったというテウフィクの研究を紹介します。VPの前で自分を小さく見せて失敗し、「レシート」ファイルを作ったダニエルの話、聞く側が価値を足し戻す日本の謙遜と、小さく言うと文字どおりに受け取られるアメリカの会議の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 自分の仕事の証拠を3つ書き出す。気持ちではなく事実で：数字、結果、誰かに言われたこと。

episodes.title: Saying No Without Burning Bridges
episodes.summary: Two days before her first presentation to Mark's team, a late-night Slack message asks Sena for a twelve-month breakdown that would take three days, and her "Of course!" reply is waiting on the send button. Daniel shares research by Givi and Kirk, where people who said no overestimated how upset the other person would be, and by Zauberman and Lynch, where people expected more free time next month than today. He tells the story of the one-line no that came back to him six months later, and they compare soft Japanese refusals like "it's a little difficult" with the US view that a late no hurts trust more than an early one. Today's challenge: say no to one request today and offer one alternative with it.

episodes.title: Perfectionism vs. Good Enough
episodes.summary: Eight minutes before Kato-san's 3 p.m. deadline for the slides Laura wants to see, Sena is on version thirteen, moving one arrow two pixels left and right, with a "tomorrow morning" request waiting in her message box. Today's challenge: decide to ship one task at eighty percent and send it before the deadline.
episodes.practice: Pick one task today and decide to ship it at eighty percent. Before you start, write down what must be right (and what is only nice to have), set a stop time before the deadline, and send it then with one line inviting feedback.
sources: Harari, Swider, Steed & Breidenthal (2018), Is Perfect Good? A Meta-Analysis of Perfectionism in the Workplace, Journal of Applied Psychology

episodes.title: Self-Compassion at Work
episodes.summary: Sena's ten-minute presentation to Mark's team went well ("This is exactly what we needed"), but in the Q&A she froze for seven seconds on one English sentence and said "two weeks" when Wendell's region three numbers need three, and Wendell corrected her in the chat. That night she replays the recording again and again, until Daniel asks what she would tell her friend Misaki after the same meeting. He shares Breines and Chen's experiments, where students who read three self-compassionate sentences after failing a test studied about 50% longer, and Grossmann and Kross's "Solomon's paradox," where people reasoned more wisely about a friend's problem than their own until they used their own name. Daniel tells how joking about his own mistake for months taught his team that mistakes follow you, and they compare Japan's "be strict with yourself, kind to others" with the American "give yourself some grace." episodes.practice: On a day something goes wrong, write yourself the same words you'd write to a friend: three sentences, using your own name. The facts, said kindly; who else has been there; and one next step.

episodes.summary: On Friday morning in Tokyo, Sena joins her first weekly video sync with Mark's team, and when Mark jokes "Let's not let that become four!" about the region three timeline, Wendell goes still, answers "Yep" and "It's in the doc," and turns his camera off. Kraus (2017), Voice-Only Communication Enhances Empathic Accuracy, American Psychologist

episodes.title: Staying Calm When Others Aren't
episodes.summary: On a voice-only call at ten in the morning in Tokyo, Wendell is angry that Mark still wants a rough cut of region three "next Friday" after he said three weeks three times, and Sena's first instinct, "I'm sure Mark didn't mean it like that," makes it worse until she says back what she heard in his words. Daniel shares Seehausen and colleagues' small Berlin study, where paraphrasing during a real conflict left people feeling less negative and speaking more quietly, and Weger and colleagues' study of 115 students, where active listening made people feel more understood than advice or simple acknowledgments. He tells the story of Bram, who told him "You're answering a question I didn't ask," and they compare Japanese aizuchi and "maa maa" with the American "What I'm hearing is..." Today's challenge: when someone sounds upset today, say back what you heard in one sentence, in their words, before you reassure or advise.

sources: Seehausen, Kazzer, Bajbouj & Prehn (2012), Effects of Empathic Paraphrasing – Extrinsic Emotion Regulation in Social Conflict, Frontiers in Psychology
Weger, Castle Bell, Minei & Robinson (2014), The Relative Effectiveness of Active Listening in Initial Interactions, International Journal of Listening

episodes.title: Gratitude That Isn't Generic

8人に同じ一文のカードを書いたダニエルの失敗
「すみません」「お疲れさま」と「Thanks!! You rock!」
episodes.summary_ja: 月曜の朝、セナはデータチェックのログを開きます。発表の2時間前、ケンタさんがこっそりスライドの全数字を再チェックしてくれていたのに、返したのは「Thanks!」の一言だけ。感謝を伝える人は、相手のうれしさや、内容への驚きを低く見積もるというクマーとエプリーの研究と、自分の得より「あなたがしてくれたこと」を言う文が大事だったというアルゴーたちの研究を紹介します。チーム8人に同じ一文のカードを書いてしまったダニエルの失敗談、「すみません」「お疲れさま」の日本と、勢いのある「Thanks!!」のアメリカの比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日、具体的な感謝のメッセージを1通送る。相手が何をしたか、それで何ができたか、そこから相手のどんなところが見えたかを短く書き、静かな人には個別に送る。
episodes.thumb_sub: Say What They Did, Make It Specific

episodes.title: Your Emotional Baseline
episodes.summary: On Tuesday morning on a bench by the moat in Tokyo, Sena counts the stress signals in her notebook margins: thirty-four notes in two weeks, twenty-two about speaking English, zero about the numbers, and six workdays with no note at all, two days after telling her mother these were the hardest two weeks of her life. In the Season Two finale, Daniel shares Kahneman and colleagues' Day Reconstruction Method study, where 909 employed women rebuilt one workday scene by scene, and Diener, Lucas and Scollon's review showing that happiness set points aren't neutral, differ between people, and can change. He tells the story of the terrible March when he almost quit managing, and they compare Japan's "daijoubu" with America's "Great!" Today's challenge: write one word a day for a week and look back.
episodes.practice: Before you leave work today, write one word for how today felt. Set a reminder for the same time every day this week. On the seventh day, read all seven words and ask: what's my usual, and what's the pattern?
sources: Kahneman, Krueger, Schkade, Schwarz & Stone (2004), A Survey Method for Characterizing Daily Life Experience: The Day Reconstruction Method, Science
Diener, Lucas & Scollon (2006), Beyond the Hedonic Treadmill: Revising the Adaptation Theory of Well-Being, American Psychologist
episodes.yt_title: Find Your Emotional Baseline with One Word a Day
episodes.hook:
You're sure the last two weeks were the worst of your life. But can you remember the quiet days?
Learn how one word a day shows your real emotional baseline: your usual weather, not your worst storm.
points: Rebuilding one day scene by scene: negative feelings were relatively infrequent and mild (Kahneman et al.)
Happiness set points aren't neutral, differ between people, and can change over years (Diener, Lucas & Scollon)
Daniel's terrible March, and the director who asked how many good weeks he'd had
Japan's "daijoubu" vs America's "Great!"
episodes.title_ja: 自分の感情のベースライン
episodes.hook_ja:
「人生でいちばんきつい2週間だった」。でも、その中の静かな日を思い出せますか？
1日1語の記録で、いちばんひどい嵐ではなく「いつものお天気」を見つける方法を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 1日をシーンごとに振り返ると、つらい気持ちは思ったより少なかった
幸せのセットポイントは中立じゃないし、人によって違い、変わりうる
マネジメントを辞めかけたダニエルの「最悪の3月」
日本の「大丈夫」とアメリカの「Great!」
episodes.summary_ja: 火曜の朝、お堀沿いのベンチで、セナはノートの余白に書いたストレスのサインを数えます。2週間で34個、そのうち22個は英語で話すこと、数字のことはゼロ。そして10日の出勤日のうち6日はメモがありませんでした。シーズン2の最終回。働く女性909人に前日を1シーンずつ組み立て直してもらったカーネマンたちの研究と、幸せのセットポイントは中立ではなく、人によって違い、変わりうるというディーナーたちのレビューを紹介します。マネジメントを辞めかけたダニエルの「最悪の3月」の話、日本の「大丈夫」とアメリカの「Great!」の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日仕事を終える前に、今日の気分を1語で書く。1週間、毎日同じ時間に続け、7日目に7つの言葉を読み返して「自分の普段」と「パターン」を見つける。
episodes.thumb_sub: One Word a Day, Find Your Usual Weather
thumb_notes: Usual weather, not the worst storm

episodes.title: Small Talk Is Not Small
episodes.summary: On a Tuesday night in her kitchen, Sena rehearses small talk with her kettle and stops after eight seconds. Kato-san has told her Laura laughed when he said Sena likes to talk about work, and the team lunch is Monday at 12:15. In the first episode of Season Three, Daniel shares Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson and Gino's study of 398 strangers chatting for fifteen minutes, where people who asked more questions, especially follow-up questions, were liked more and didn't expect it, and Kardas, Kumar and Epley's ten experiments showing that people expect conversations with strangers to be more awkward than they are. He tells the story of a dinner with a visiting vice president where he asked twelve work questions and no follow-up, and they compare Japan's shared greetings like "samuku narimashita ne" with American small talk. Today's challenge: in the first two minutes of one meeting, ask a non-task question and one follow-up.
episodes.practice: In the first two minutes of one meeting or conversation today, ask one question that isn't about the task. After their answer, ask one follow-up question about something they just said.
sources: Huang, Yeomans, Brooks, Minson & Gino (2017), It Doesn't Hurt to Ask: Question-Asking Increases Liking, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
Kardas, Kumar & Epley (2022), Overly Shallow?: Miscalibrated Expectations Create a Barrier to Deeper Conversation, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
episodes.yt_title: Small Talk Is Not Small: Two Questions and One Follow-Up
episodes.hook:
Small talk feels like empty air until the silence arrives. But the people who ask more follow-up questions are liked more, and they don't see it coming.
Learn two questions and one follow-up for the first two minutes of any conversation.
points: People who asked more questions were liked more, and the askers didn't expect it (Huang et al.)
Follow-up questions signal "I heard you"
Strangers expect conversations to be more awkward than they are (Kardas, Kumar & Epley)
Daniel's dinner: twelve work questions, zero follow-ups
Japan's shared greetings vs American small talk
episodes.title_ja: 雑談は、小さくない
episodes.hook_ja:
雑談はただの空気のように感じるけれど、沈黙が来ると困りますよね。実は、フォローアップ質問が多い人ほど好かれやすいのに、本人はそれに気づいていません。
どんな会話の最初の2分でも使える「質問2つ＋フォローアップ1つ」を英語で学ぼう🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: たくさん質問した人ほど好かれたが、質問した側はそれを予想していなかった
フォローアップ質問は「ちゃんと聞いてたよ」のサイン
知らない人との会話は、思うより気まずくない
ダニエルのディナー：仕事の質問12個、フォローアップはゼロ
日本の共通のあいさつとアメリカの雑談
episodes.summary_ja: 火曜の夜、台所でセナはやかん相手に雑談の練習をして、8秒で止まってしまいます。加藤さんによると、セナは仕事の話が好きだと言ったらローラに笑われたそうで、チームのランチは月曜12時15分です。シーズン3の最初の回。398人の知らない人どうしが15分チャットした実験で、たくさん質問した人、特にフォローアップ質問をした人ほど好かれ、本人はそれを予想していなかったというホアンたちの研究と、知らない人との会話は思ったより気まずくないというカーダスたちの10の実験を紹介します。来訪中の副社長に仕事の質問を12個して、フォローアップを1つもしなかったダニエルの失敗談、「寒くなりましたね」のような日本の共通のあいさつとアメリカの雑談の比較も。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日、会議や会話の最初の2分に、仕事以外の質問を1つする。相手の答えのあと、相手が今言ったことについてフォローアップ質問を1つする。
episodes.thumb_sub: Two Questions, One Follow-Up, in Two Minutes

episodes.title: Explain It Without the Slides
episodes.summary: Sena practices explaining how she thinks about numbers to her friend Aoi, a nurse, who says she understood four words out of twenty-one. Laura has asked for an informal explanation with no slides at Monday's lunch. Daniel shares Pamela Hinds's curse-of-expertise LEGO study: people who had built the toy five times guessed first-timers would need about 8.5 minutes, while real first-timers needed about 12.5, and a list of tips barely changed their guesses. He tells the story of Leona, a finance partner who nodded through forty minutes of his attrition model and then cut his hiring request in half. In the Japan-vs-US centerpiece, Sena replays a Tokyo report meeting where the number arrives after seven minutes of keii (background) and a Seattle call where Laura says "What's the number, and what do you need from us?" Today's challenge: explain one thing you do to someone outside your field in three sentences, then ask what part didn't land. It ends with Kato-san's message at 7:51 a.m.: Laura has one question for Sena on the eight o'clock call, no prep.
episodes.practice: Pick one thing you do at work and explain it to someone outside your field in three sentences: the question it answers, one example, and what it means for them. Then ask, "What part didn't land?"
sources: Hinds (1999), The Curse of Expertise: The Effects of Expertise and Debiasing Methods on Prediction of Novice Performance, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Applied 5(2), 205–221; Hinds (1998), Who Should Design for Novice Users?, HP Laboratories report HPL-98-136
episodes.yt_title: Experts Can't Explain Things Simply. Here's a One-Minute Fix
episodes.hook:
The more you know, the worse you are at guessing what it's like not to know. People who built a LEGO toy five times guessed beginners needed 8.5 minutes. They needed 12.5.
Learn a three-sentence way to explain your work to anyone, no slides.
points: Experts underestimated beginners' time by nearly four minutes (Hinds)
A list of beginner problems barely changed experts' guesses
Nodding can mean "please stop," not "I understand"
Tokyo: background first so nobody is surprised. Seattle: bottom line first to protect time
Headline plus an offer: "Want the background, or an example?"
episodes.title_ja: スライドなしで説明する
episodes.hook_ja:
よく知っている人ほど、知らない人の感覚を予想できません。レゴを5回作った人は、初心者に8.5分かかると予想しましたが、実際は12.5分でした。
どんな人にも、スライドなしで3文で仕事を説明する方法を紹介します🎧（日本語字幕あり）
points_ja: 専門家は初心者の所要時間を4分近く短く見積もった（ハインズ）
初心者のつまずきのリストを渡しても、予想はほとんど変わらなかった
うなずきは「わかった」ではなく「もうやめて」のことも
東京は背景が先で驚きを防ぎ、シアトルは結論が先で時間を守る
結論＋提案：「背景を聞きますか？それとも例を挙げましょうか？」
episodes.summary_ja: セナは数字の考え方を友だちの看護師アオイに説明して、21語中4語しかわからなかったと言われます。ローラは月曜のランチで、スライドなしの気軽な説明を求めています。ダニエルは、パメラ・ハインズの「専門知識の呪い」の研究を紹介します。レゴを5回作った人は初心者に約8.5分かかると予想し、本物の初心者は約12.5分でした。ダニエルの失敗談は、財務のレオナに離職モデルを40分説明して、うなずかれたまま採用リクエストを半分に削られた話。日米の見せ場では、7分の経緯のあとにやっと数字が出る東京の報告会と、「数字はいくつで、何をしてほしいの？」と聞くシアトルの会議を比べます。今日のチャレンジは、仕事の1つを分野外の人に3文で説明し、「どの部分が伝わらなかった？」と聞くこと。最後は加藤さんから、ローラが8時の会議でセナに準備なしの質問があるという連絡で終わります。
episodes.practice_ja: 仕事で自分がやっていることを1つ選び、自分の分野の外の人に3文で説明する。それが答える問い、例を1つ、相手にとっての意味。そして「どの部分が伝わらなかった？」と聞く。
episodes.thumb_sub: Explain Your Thinking in One Minute, No Slides
thumb_notes: Say what it means for them

episodes.title: Buying Time Before You Answer
episodes.summary: On Thursday at 8 a.m., Laura asks Sena in front of eleven people what breaks first if the region three dashboard launches two weeks early, and the call goes quiet. Daniel shares Stivers and colleagues' 2009 study of ten languages, where the average wait before answering a yes-or-no question was about 200 milliseconds and non-answers came slower than answers, with honest limits about casual talk. He tells the story of Warren, a VP in a hallway who got a one-second "Yes, sure" and a launch seven weeks late. Japan vs the US: six seconds of silence and "Sou desu ne" in a Tokyo meeting, "Kentou shimasu," and a frozen face on Mark's video call. Sena shares what she said to Laura. Today's challenge: when you can't answer yet, say "Let me think about that for a second," breathe once, then answer or say what you know, what you don't, and when you'll know.
episodes.practice: The next time someone asks you something you can't answer yet, say "Let me think about that for a second." Take one breath. Then answer, or say what you know, what you don't know yet, and when you'll know.
sources: Stivers, Enfield, Brown, Englert, Hayashi, Heinemann, Hoymann, Rossano, de Ruiter, Yoon & Levinson (2009), Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
episodes.yt_title: Put on the Spot in a Meeting? What to Say Before You Answer
episodes.hook:
Someone asks a hard question and the room goes quiet. A pause with no label is easy to misread.
Here is the one sentence that makes three seconds of silence work for you.
points: In casual talk, people answer yes-or-no questions in about a fifth of a second on average (Stivers et al.)
In all ten languages, non-answers came slower than answers
A pause with no label is open to interpretation
Daniel's one-second "Yes, sure" cost seven weeks
Silence in a Tokyo room vs silence on a video call
episodes.title_ja: 答える前に、時間を買う
episodes.hook_ja:
難しい質問をされて、部屋がしんとなる。ラベルのない間は、誤解されやすい。
3秒の沈黙を味方にする、たった一つの言い方を紹介します。
points_ja: くだけた会話では、イエス・ノーの質問に平均約5分の1秒で答える（スティバーズたち）
10の言語すべてで、答えでない返事は答えより遅かった
ラベルのない間は、どう受け取られるかわからない
ダニエルの1秒の「はい、もちろん」は7週間の遅れになった
東京の部屋での沈黙と、ビデオ通話での沈黙
episodes.summary_ja: 木曜の朝8時、ローラが11人の前でセナに「リージョン3のダッシュボードを2週間前倒ししたら、最初に何が壊れる？」と聞き、通話がしんとなります。ダニエルは、スティバーズたちの10言語の研究を紹介します。イエス・ノーの質問に答えるまでの平均は約200ミリ秒で、答えでない返事は答えより遅かったそうです（くだけた会話という限界も正直に）。廊下で1秒の「はい、もちろん」と答えて、7週間遅れになったVP、ウォーレンの話。日本とアメリカでは、東京の会議の6秒の沈黙と「そうですね」、「検討します」、マークのビデオ通話で固まった顔を比べます。セナはローラに何と答えたのか。今日のチャレンジ：すぐ答えられないときは「ちょっと考えさせてください」と言って息を1回、そのあと答えるか、わかっていること、わからないこと、いつわかるかを伝える。
episodes.practice_ja: 次に、まだ答えられないことを聞かれたら、「ちょっと考えさせてください」と言う。息を1回。そして答えるか、わかっていること、わからないこと、いつわかるかを伝える。
episodes.thumb_sub: The One Sentence for Three Seconds of Silence

episodes.title: Asking Clarifying Questions
episodes.summary: On Friday night Sena sends Mark a dashboard she spent a day on, and he replies that he meant "the other thing" by "actionable." She had been afraid to ask. Daniel shares Dingemanse and colleagues' 2015 study of about 48.5 hours of informal talk in twelve languages, where someone signaled "I didn't get that" about once every 1.4 minutes and people chose the most specific question they could, with honest limits about casual conversation. He tells the story of Imogen, a director who asked him to be "more visible" and wanted two minutes at an executive review, not a thirty-slide deck. Japan vs the US: "Yoroshiku onegaishimasu" and the secret second meeting in Tokyo, "Great question!" in Seattle, and the shared fear of asking a vice president. Today's challenge: when someone gives you a vague request, say "Just to make sure I understand, you want X by Y. Is that right?"
episodes.practice: Once today, when someone gives you a vague request, say back what you heard: "Just to make sure I understand, you want X by Y. Is that right?" Then wait for the answer.
sources: Dingemanse, Roberts, Baranova, Blythe, Drew, Floyd et al. (2015), Universal Principles in the Repair of Communication Problems, PLOS ONE
episodes.yt_title: Got a Vague Request? Ask This Without Sounding Lost
episodes.hook:
"Make it more actionable." "Be more visible." You nod, guess, and find out too late.
Here is a one-sentence way to check what someone means, and why it's cheaper than guessing.
points: Someone signals "I didn't get that" about once every 1.4 minutes, in every language studied (Dingemanse et al.)
People choose the most specific question they can
A guess ("You mean Friday?") is the cheapest kind
Daniel's three weeks on the wrong thing for Imogen
Asking in Tokyo vs Seattle, and the fear that crosses both
episodes.title_ja: あいまいな依頼を、聞き返す
episodes.hook_ja:
「もっとアクショナブルに」「もっと見えるように」。うなずいて、推測して、あとで気づく。
相手の言いたいことを確認する一文と、推測するより安く済む理由を紹介します。
points_ja: 人は約1.4分に1回「わからなかった」と合図する、調べたどの言語でも（ディンゲマンスたち）
人はできるだけ具体的な質問を選ぶ
推測を出す質問（「金曜のこと？」）がいちばん安い
ダニエルがイモージェンのために3週間かけた、違うもの
東京とシアトルでの聞き方と、どちらにもある怖さ
episodes.summary_ja: 金曜の夜、セナは一日かけたダッシュボードをマークに送り、「アクショナブル」は「別のこと」を言いたかったと返されます。聞くのが怖かったのです。ダニエルは、ディンゲマンスたちの2015年の研究を紹介します。12の言語、約48時間半のくだけた会話で、約1.4分に1回「わからなかった」の合図があり、人はできるだけ具体的な質問を選んでいました（くだけた会話という限界も正直に）。「もっと見えるように」と言われて30枚のスライドを作ったのに、経営レビューで2分話してほしかっただけだったディレクター、イモージェンの話。日本とアメリカでは、「よろしくお願いします」と秘密の2回目の会議、「いい質問！」、副社長に聞く怖さを比べます。今日のチャレンジ：あいまいな依頼に「確認させてください。XをYまでに、ということですね。合っていますか？」と言う。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日一度、あいまいな依頼をされたら、聞いたことを言い返す。「確認させてください。XをYまでに、ということですね。合っていますか？」そして答えを待つ。
episodes.thumb_sub: Check What They Mean in One Sentence
episodes.thumb_cup: Say it back, ask if it's right

episodes.title: Interrupting Politely
episodes.summary: At a Monday meeting in Tokyo with Laura in the room, Kato-san guesses "probably seasonal" about slide four while Ryo freezes, and Sena has about three seconds to step in. She waits for a gap that never comes, then asks Ryo, not the room, "Can I add something?" and explains in ten seconds that the April report and the new check count returned orders differently. Daniel shares Katherine Hilton's Stanford research on how American English listeners hear overlapping speech differently (500 listeners; a later survey of about 5,000 as reported by Stanford), with honest limits. He tells the story of Tobias, a VP who locked a launch date into the holiday code freeze while Daniel waited politely for a pause that never came. Japan vs the US: the soft "Sumimasen, hitotsu dake yoroshii deshou ka?" and aizuchi in Tokyo, the "quick add" flag in Seattle, and how Americans can open the door for Tokyo colleagues. Today's challenge: step in once with "Can I add something?", say one thing in about ten seconds, then hand it back.
episodes.practice: Once today, in a meeting, a call or a group chat, step in with "Can I add something?" Say one thing, about ten seconds, on the same topic and at the same volume, then hand it back: "That's all. Back to you."
sources: Hilton (2016), The Perception of Overlapping Speech: Effects of Speaker Prosody and Listener Attitudes, Proceedings of Interspeech 2016
Stanford Report (May 2, 2018), Stanford researcher examines how people perceive interruptions in conversation (Hilton's survey of about 5,000 American English speakers)
episodes.yt_title: Can't Get a Word In? How to Jump In Without Being Rude
episodes.hook:
The conversation moves faster than your courage. You wait for a gap, and the meeting moves on.
Here is a ten-second way to step in without stepping on anyone, and what research says about who hears an interruption.
points: The same words are heard as rude or engaged depending on the listener (Hilton, Stanford)
Ask the person you are about to interrupt, not the room
One thing, about ten seconds, same topic, no louder voice, then hand it back
Daniel's wait for a pause that never came, and the code freeze
Tokyo's soft ask and aizuchi vs Seattle's "quick add" flag
episodes.title_ja: 割って入る、感じよく
episodes.hook_ja:
会話は、あなたの勇気より速く進む。すき間を待つあいだに、会議は先へ行ってしまう。
誰の足も踏まずに入る、10秒の方法と、誰が割り込みと感じるのかについての研究を紹介します。
points_ja: 同じ言葉でも、聞き手しだいで失礼にも前向きにも聞こえる（ヒルトン、スタンフォード）
割り込む相手に、部屋ではなくその人に聞く
ひとつだけ、10秒くらい、同じ話題で、声は大きくせず、そして返す
ダニエルが来ない間を待った話と、コード凍結
東京のやわらかい一言とあいづち、シアトルの「quick add」という合図
episodes.summary_ja: 東京での月曜の会議。ローラさんが同席する中、4枚目のスライドについて加藤さんが「たぶん季節要因」と推測を言い、リョウさんが固まります。セナに使える時間は約3秒。来ないすき間を待ったあと、部屋ではなくリョウさんに「Can I add something?」と聞き、4月のレポートと新しいチェックで返品の数え方が違うことを10秒で説明します。ダニエルは、アメリカ英語の聞き手が重なる発話をどう聞くかについての、スタンフォードのキャサリン・ヒルトンの研究を紹介します（500人の実験と、スタンフォードの記事で報じられた約5000人の調査。限界も正直に）。そして、年末のコード凍結期間にリリース日を確定させたVP、トバイアスの前で、来ない間を礼儀正しく待ち続けた自分の失敗談。日本とアメリカでは、東京のそっと入る「ひとつだけよろしいでしょうか」とあいづち、シアトルの「quick add」という合図、そしてアメリカの人が東京の同僚のためにドアを開ける方法を比べます。今日のチャレンジ：「Can I add something?」で一度入り、10秒でひとつ話して、返す。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日一度、会議でも通話でもグループチャットでも、「Can I add something?」で入る。同じ話題で、同じ声の大きさで、ひとつだけ10秒ほど話して、返す。「以上です。お返しします。」
episodes.thumb_sub: Step Into a Conversation in Ten Seconds

episodes.title: Listen, Summarize, Then Speak
episodes.summary: At a Monday lunch in Tokyo, Laura talks for four minutes about her worries over region three and then asks Sena what she thinks. Instead of giving five fixes, Sena takes a breath and says back the worry underneath, that nobody owns the word "ready," and asks "Did I get that right?" Daniel shares Yeomans, Minson and colleagues' 2020 study of conversational receptiveness (771 writers, 1,548 raters): replies that acknowledged understanding, found agreement and hedged were rated more receptive and a bit more persuasive, with honest limits about online strangers and political topics. He tells the story of Dmitri and Soraya, where his summary of a forty-minute debate was really his own view and cost the team three weeks. Japan vs the US: fukushou, repeating back, in Tokyo restaurants and phone calls, which checks facts but not worries, versus "What I'm hearing is..." in Seattle, which can sound like technique, and how Laura's "What did we decide?" summarizes the outcome but not the person. Today's challenge: before you give your opinion, say the other person's point with their reason in one sentence and ask "Did I get that right?"
episodes.practice: Once today, before you give your opinion, say the other person's point in one sentence, with their reason ("You're worried about X because Y"), and ask, "Did I get that right?" Then say your view.
sources: Yeomans, Minson, Collins, Chen & Gino (2020), Conversational receptiveness: Improving engagement with opposing views, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 160, 131–148
episodes.yt_title: Want Your Pushback to Land? Say Their Point First
episodes.hook:
You have the answer ready, and so does everyone else. Before you give it, there is one sentence that shows you were listening.
Here is how to say someone's point back, with their reason, and what research says it does for how you are heard.
points: Replies that said "I understand" first were rated more receptive and a bit more persuasive (Yeomans et al., 771 writers, 1,548 raters)
Say their reason, not only their words: "You're worried about X because Y"
Daniel's summary that was really his own opinion, and Dmitri's quiet vendor demo
Tokyo's fukushou checks facts, not worries; Seattle's "What I'm hearing is" can sound like technique
Then ask "Did I get that right?" and let them say no
episodes.title_ja: 聞いて、要約して、それから話す
episodes.hook_ja:
答えは用意できている。ほかのみんなも同じ。それを言う前に、「聞いていた」と伝える一文があります。
相手の話を、相手の理由と一緒に言い返す方法と、それが伝わり方にもたらすことについての研究を紹介します。
points_ja: 先に「わかります」と言った返信は、より受け入れる姿勢があり、説得力も少し高いと評価された（ヨーマンズたち、書き手771人・評価者1548人）
言葉だけでなく理由を言う。「Yが理由で、Xが心配なんですね」
ダニエルの、実は自分の意見だった要約と、ドミトリの静かなベンダーデモ
東京の復唱は事実を確かめ、心配は確かめない。シアトルの「What I'm hearing is」はテクニックに聞こえることがある
最後に「合っていますか？」と聞いて、相手が「違う」と言えるようにする
episodes.summary_ja: 月曜の東京でのランチ。ローラさんがリージョン3の不安を4分間話し、セナに「どう思う？」と聞きます。セナは5つの解決策を出す代わりに、一呼吸おいて、その下にある心配、「誰も『準備できた』を持っていない」ことを言い返し、「合っていますか？」と聞きます。ダニエルは、ヨーマンズ、ミンソンたちの2020年の研究「Conversational receptiveness」（書き手771人、評価者1548人）を紹介します。「わかります」と伝え、同意できる点を見つけ、ぼかして書いた返信は、より受け入れる姿勢があり、説得力も少し高いと評価されました（相手はオンラインの見知らぬ人で政治的なテーマ、という限界も正直に）。そして、40分の議論の要約が実は自分の意見で、チームに3週間のむだをさせた、ドミトリとソラヤの話。日本とアメリカでは、東京のお店や電話での「復唱」が事実は確かめても心配は確かめないこと、シアトルの「What I'm hearing is…」がテクニックに聞こえうること、ローラさんの「What did we decide?」が結果は要約しても人は要約しないことを比べます。今日のチャレンジ：自分の意見を言う前に、相手の話を理由と一緒に一文で言い、「合っていますか？」と聞く。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日一度、自分の意見を言う前に、相手の話を、相手の理由と一緒に一文で言う（「Yが理由で、Xが心配なんですね」）。そして「Did I get that right?」と聞く。そのあとで、自分の考えを言う。
episodes.thumb_sub: Show You Heard Before You Disagree
thumb_notes: Ask: did I get that right?

episodes.title: Retell in 30 Seconds
episodes.summary: Laura asks Sena for thirty seconds on region three at a leadership sync. The night before, Sena had read her fourteen pages six times and felt ready, but when she closed the notebook and retold the month from memory she couldn't say Wendell's date. Kato-san's hallway question, "what to worry about this week, and what to do about it," turns it into three sentences: where it stands, what could break, what I need. Daniel shares Roediger and Karpicke's 2006 testing-effect study (120 and 180 undergraduates): retelling from memory beat rereading after two days and a week even though rereading won at five minutes, with honest limits about students, short passages and written recall. He tells the story of Hector, a director who asked "Is the project late?" after Daniel saved the bad news for the end of a day-by-day update. Japan vs the US: "ketsuron kara itte" versus keii, the background that comes first in Tokyo emails, versus bottom line up front in many American companies, plus Laura's one-line "Bottom line?" and Kato-san's twelve-words-on-top fix. Today's challenge: after one meeting, close your notes and say the main point out loud in thirty seconds, record it, then check what you dropped and added.
episodes.practice: After one meeting or call today, close your notes and say the main point out loud in thirty seconds: where it stands, what could break, what you need. Record it on your phone, then open your notes and see what you dropped and what you added.
sources: Roediger & Karpicke (2006), Test-Enhanced Learning: Taking Memory Tests Improves Long-Term Retention, Psychological Science 17(3), 249–255
episodes.yt_title: Asked for a Quick Update? Say It in 30 Seconds
episodes.hook:
Someone says "Give me the quick version," and your whole month tries to come out at once. You have thirty seconds and fourteen pages.
Here is a three-sentence way to retell any meeting or project, and a simple test for what you actually remember.
points: Rereading felt better at five minutes; retelling from memory won at two days and a week (Roediger & Karpicke, 120 and 180 students)
Close your notes and say it out loud: you find what you really know
Where it stands, what could break, what I need (with a name and a day)
Daniel's day-by-day update and Hector's "Is the project late?"
Tokyo's background first vs Seattle's bottom line first: put the conclusion on top and the background underneath
episodes.title_ja: 30秒で話し直す
episodes.hook_ja:
「ざっくり教えて」と言われて、1か月ぶんが一度に出てこようとする。30秒しかなくて、ノートは14ページ。
どんな会議やプロジェクトも話し直せる三つの文の型と、自分が本当に覚えていることを確かめる簡単なテストを紹介します。
points_ja: 読み直しは5分後は有利でも、記憶から話し直すほうが、2日後と1週間後に勝った（ローディガーとカーピキ、学生120人と180人）
ノートを閉じて声に出す。本当に知っていることが見える
いまどこか、何が崩れうるか、何が必要か（名前と日付つきで）
ダニエルの日ごとの報告と、ヘクターの「プロジェクトは遅れてるのか？」
東京の経緯が先と、シアトルの結論が先。結論を上に、経緯を下に置く
episodes.summary_ja: リーダーシップ会議で、ローラさんがセナにリージョン3について30秒を求めます。前の晩、セナは14ページを6回読んで準備できたと思っていたのに、ノートを閉じて1か月ぶんを記憶から話し直したら、ウェンデルさんの日付が出てきませんでした。加藤さんが廊下で言った「今週何を心配すべきか、そしてそれにどうするか」を手がかりに、三つの文、いまどこまで来たか、何が崩れうるか、何が必要か、にまとめます。ダニエルは、ローディガーとカーピキの2006年のテスト効果の研究（学部生120人と180人）を紹介します。読み直しは5分後には勝ったのに、記憶から話し直したほうが2日後と1週間後に勝ちました（学生、短い文章、書いて思い出す形という限界も正直に）。そして、日ごとの報告の最後に悪い知らせをとっておいて、ディレクターのヘクターに「プロジェクトは遅れてるのか？」と聞かれた話。日本とアメリカでは、「結論から言って」と、東京のメールで先に来る経緯、アメリカの多くの会社の「結論を先に」を比べ、ローラさんの一行の「Bottom line?」と、加藤さんの「上に12語、下に参考」という工夫も紹介します。今日のチャレンジ：ひとつ会議のあと、ノートを閉じて要点を30秒で声に出し、録音して、何を落として何を足したか確認する。
episodes.practice_ja: 今日、会議か通話をひとつ終えたら、ノートを閉じて、要点を30秒で声に出す。いまどこか、何が崩れうるか、何が必要か。スマホで録音して、そのあとノートを開き、何を落として何を足したかを見てみる。
episodes.thumb_sub: Retell Any Meeting in 30 Seconds

episodes.title: Speaking Before You Feel Ready
episodes.summary: Thursday's call has Mark's whole launch team, eleven people Sena has never met, and Laura wants her to open it. After a perfect three-paragraph opening that begins with an apology, Sena writes only one specific first sentence, rates her nerves in the margin (7 at midnight, 8 at 7:58), and opens with a line about marketing's banner. Her nerves go to 5 after the sentence and 3 by minute ten. Daniel shares Savitsky and Gilovich's 2003 illusion-of-transparency studies: 40 Cornell students rated themselves as looking more nervous (6.55) than their partners did (5.25), and speakers told about the illusion were rated more composed and gave better speeches than speakers who got nothing or plain reassurance (77 speakers), with honest limits, including a 2011 master's thesis with 31 anxious students that found no significant differences. He tells the story of Lucia, who said his on-call idea half-baked in minute three while he waited for his numbers. Japan vs the US: "Nanika goiken wa arimasu ka?" and a seven-second silence in Tokyo, where the meeting confirms and nemawashi does the thinking, versus "Strawman" and "half-baked, but..." in Seattle, and why "ready" means two different things. Today's challenge: say one sentence in the first minute of your next meeting and write your nerves, 1 to 10, before and after.
episodes.practice: In your next meeting, say one sentence in the first minute, before you feel ready. Write your nerves from one to ten before and after, and use a rough opener if you need one: "Here's a rough thought," or "Can I start with one thing?"
sources: Savitsky & Gilovich (2003), The illusion of transparency and the alleviation of speech anxiety, Journal of Experimental Social Psychology 39(6), 618–625
Gloth (2011), The Illusion of Transparency and Public Speaking: A Study of Social Anxiety, master's thesis, Minnesota State University, Mankato (small replication attempt, 31 participants)
episodes.yt_title: Waiting to Feel Ready to Speak Up? Say One Sentence First
episodes.hook:
You are waiting to feel ready before you speak in the meeting, and the room keeps moving. Your heart is loud, and you are sure everyone can see it.
Here is why the first minute is the easiest time to speak, a one-sentence opener, and what research says about how nervous you really look.
points: People think they look more nervous than they do: 6.55 vs 5.25 (Savitsky & Gilovich, 40 students)
Speakers told about the illusion were rated more composed and gave better speeches than speakers who were just told not to worry
Write only the first sentence, with one detail only you have, and say it in the first minute
Daniel waited for his numbers; Lucia said a half-baked version of his idea in minute three
Tokyo's silence is often groundwork elsewhere; "ready" means two different things
episodes.title_ja: 準備できる前に話す
episodes.hook_ja:
準備できたと感じるまで待っているうちに、会議は先へ進む。心臓の音は大きくて、全員に見えている気がする。
最初の1分がいちばん話しやすい理由と、一文のオープナー、そして実際どれくらい緊張して見えているのかについての研究を紹介します。
points_ja: 人は、実際より緊張して見えていると思っている：6.55対5.25（サヴィツキーとギロビッチ、学生40人）
この錯覚を教えられた人は、ただ「心配しないで」と言われた人より、落ち着いて見え、スピーチも良いと評価された
最初の一文だけを書く。自分しか知らない細かい情報をひとつ入れて、最初の1分で言う
数字を待っていたダニエルと、3分目に彼のアイデアの粗いバージョンを言ったルシア
東京の沈黙は、根回しが別の場所にあることも多い。「準備できた」はふたつの意味を持つ
episodes.summary_ja: 木曜の会議には、マークさんのリリースチーム、セナが会ったことのない11人が入ってきて、ローラさんはセナに口火を切ってほしいと言います。謝罪で始まる完璧な3段落のオープニングを書いたあと、セナは、具体的な最初の一文だけを書き、余白に緊張を記録します（夜中は7、7時58分は8）。そして、マーケティングのバナーの話で始めます。緊張は、その一文のあとに5、10分後には3。ダニエルは、サヴィツキーとギロビッチの2003年の「透明性の錯覚」の研究を紹介します。コーネル大学の学生40人は、自分のほうが相手より緊張して見えたと評価し（6.55対5.25）、この錯覚を教えられた話し手は、何も言われなかった人やただ安心させられた人より、落ち着いて見え、スピーチも良いと評価されました（話し手77人）。限界も正直に、2011年のミネソタの修士論文（不安の強い学生31人）は有意な差を見つけませんでした。そして、数字を待っているあいだに、3分目にルシアが彼のオンコール案を粗い形で言ってしまった話。日本とアメリカでは、東京の「何かご意見はありませんか？」と7秒の沈黙（会議は確認の場で、考える作業は根回しで）と、シアトルの「Strawman」「まだ半分ですが…」を比べ、「準備できた」がふたつの意味を持つことを見ます。今日のチャレンジ：次の会議の最初の1分で一文を言い、緊張を1から10で前後に記録する。
episodes.practice_ja: 次の会議で、準備できた気持ちになる前に、最初の1分で一文を言う。緊張を、1から10で、前と後に書く。必要なら、粗い始め方を使う。「Here's a rough thought」や「Can I start with one thing?」。

thumb_notes: Add one detail only you have
Say it in the first minute

episodes.title: Presenting with a Story
episodes.summary: Laura wants three minutes from Sena at next Wednesday's Seattle product review: "No chart on slide one. Start with a person." Sena has fourteen pages and no person. Kato-san tells her to call Tanabe-san, an Osaka store manager who builds her weekly numbers by hand. At 7:40 a.m. Sena calls her; Tanabe-san says to use her name and tells her about Sunday nights: ninety minutes of copying six days of sales, and last Sunday at eleven she found she had typed Tuesday twice. Daniel shares Small, Loewenstein and Slovic's 2007 study: 159 people on a Pennsylvania campus each earned five dollars and could donate to Save the Children; Rokia, a seven-year-old girl, drew $2.38 on average against $1.14 for statistics, and a group that saw both gave $1.43. He is honest about the limits: a charity donation, students and passersby, and a 2024 pre-registered replication that found no support for the effect, so person-first is his judgment, not the paper's. He tells the story of Pilar, who asked "Whose ticket is that?" when he saved his customer for slide thirteen. Japan vs the US: Kato-san's Osaka deck puts the customer's voice last as "Customer A" to protect the person, while Laura asks "What's her name? What did she do last Tuesday?" The skill: open with one real person (a name, a place and a moment, one detail only they gave you, then your number), after checking you heard it from them, can say it in their words, and they agreed to be named. Last challenge recap, today's one-day challenge, and a cliffhanger: Mark asks for a region three view by Monday 9 a.m. Tokyo time.
episodes.practice: Open your next talk, update or email with one real person: a name, a place and a moment, one detail only they gave you, then your number. First check that you heard it from them and that they said yes to being named.
sources: Small, Loewenstein & Slovic (2007), Sympathy and callousness: The impact of deliberative thought on donations to identifiable and statistical victims, Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes 102(2), 143–153
episodes.yt_title: Told to Start With a Person, Not a Chart? Try This
episodes.hook:
"No chart on slide one. Start with a person." Your director just said it, and you have fourteen pages of columns and nobody to point to.
Here is a four-part way to open any talk with one real person, and a test for whether your story is true enough to tell.
points: A single girl named Rokia drew $2.38 in donations vs $1.14 for statistics; adding statistics dropped it to $1.43 (Small, Loewenstein & Slovic, 159 people)
The limits: charity, students, and a 2024 replication that found no support, so person-first is a judgment call
Name, place and moment, one detail only they gave you, then your number
Daniel's slide thirteen, and Pilar's "Whose ticket is that?"
Tokyo's "Customer A" protects the person; Seattle asks "What's her name?" Ask permission first
episodes.title_ja: ストーリーで始めるプレゼン
episodes.hook_ja:
「スライド1枚目にグラフは置かないで。人から始めて。」ディレクターにそう言われたのに、手元には14ページの列と、指させる相手がいない。
どんな話も実在の一人から始められる四つの型と、その話が語れるほど本当かを確かめるテストを紹介します。
points_ja: ロキアという女の子一人は平均2.38ドル、統計は1.14ドル、両方を見せると1.43ドル（スモール、ローウェンスタイン、スロヴィック、159人）
限界：寄付の話、学生が対象、2024年の再現実験は効果を支持せず。だから「人が先」は判断
名前、場所と瞬間、その人しかくれない細かい情報、そのあとに数字
ダニエルの13枚目のスライドと、ピラールの「それは誰のチケットなの？」
東京の「A社様」は人を守る、シアトルは「名前は？」と聞く。まず許可を取る
episodes.summary_ja: ローラさんは、来週水曜のシアトルのプロダクトレビューで、セナに3分を求めます。「スライド1枚目にグラフは置かないで。人から始めて。」セナには14ページあるのに、人はいません。加藤さんは、毎週の数字を手作業で作っている大阪の店長、田辺さんに電話するよう言います。朝7時40分、セナが電話すると、田辺さんは名前を使っていいと言い、日曜の夜のことを話します。6日ぶんの売上を写すのに90分、先週の日曜は夜11時に、火曜日を2回入力していたことに気づいたそうです。ダニエルは、スモール、ローウェンスタイン、スロヴィックの2007年の研究を紹介します。ペンシルベニアのキャンパスで159人が5ドルを受け取り、セーブ・ザ・チルドレンに寄付できました。7歳の女の子ロキアには平均2.38ドル、統計には1.14ドル、両方を見たグループは1.43ドル。限界も正直に、寄付の話で、学生と通りがかりの人が対象、2024年の事前登録された再現実験は効果を支持しませんでした。だから「人が先」は論文ではなくダニエルの判断です。ダニエルの失敗談は、お客さんの話を13枚目まで取っておいて、ピラールに「それは誰のチケットなの？」と聞かれたこと。日本とアメリカでは、加藤さんの大阪時代の資料では、お客様の声は最後に「A社様」として人を守る形で置かれ、ローラさんは「名前は？先週の火曜日に何をした？」と聞きます。スキルは、実在の一人から始めること（名前、場所と瞬間、その人しかくれない細かい情報、そのあとに数字）。本人から聞いた、本人の言葉で言える、名前を出すことに合意している、の三つを確かめます。前回のチャレンジの振り返りと、今日のチャレンジ、そして最後に、マークさんが月曜の東京時間朝9時までのリージョン3のビューを求めてくる引きです。
episodes.practice_ja: 次の発表、報告、メールを、実在の一人から始める。名前、場所と瞬間、その人しかくれない細かい情報、そのあとに数字。本人から聞いた話か、名前を出していいか、先に確かめる。

thumb_notes: One detail only they gave you

episodes.title: Pushing Back on Deadlines
episodes.summary: Mark asks for a region three view by Monday 9 a.m. Tokyo time, three days of work, and Sena's draft reply is two words: "Yes, sure." She asks Kenta (region two took four days plus one to fix a filter) and Ryo (the Osaka script: two days planned, six taken), then shows Kato-san her reply: a one-page preview by Tuesday 9 a.m. her time, or the full view after Wednesday, and "Which would help more on Wednesday?" Mark answers in four seconds: "OH. One page!!" Daniel shares Buehler, Griffin and Ross's 1994 planning-fallacy study: 37 psychology students at the University of Waterloo predicted 33.9 days to finish their honors thesis and took 55.5; only 29.7% finished by their best guess and 10.8% by the optimistic date. He is honest about the limits (students, one big project, 1994; observers judging others guessed too long) and says only that your own guess is the one most likely to leave out the filter that breaks. His failure story: he told Odette two weeks for a data export that had taken five weeks before; it took thirty-four days, and Odette had already told her VP. Japan vs the US: Kato-san's "Kentou shimasu" (a polite no heard as yes) and "Nantoka shimasu" (a yes with a hidden cost) vs Laura's "What's the real deadline? What happens if it's Tuesday?", and Seattle's cheerful "Sure, no problem!" The skill: push back with an offer (what I can do and by when, what has to move, what matters most), after checking how long the last similar task took. Last challenge recap, today's one-day challenge, and a cliffhanger: Laura's three questions for Wednesday, the last of which nobody can answer, and "Please don't guess."
episodes.practice: Before you say yes to a deadline, find out how long the last similar thing really took. Then answer with what you can do by when, and ask what matters most.

episodes.title_ja: 期限に代案で押し返す
episodes.hook_ja:
「月曜の朝9時、そっちの時間で！！」返信の下書きは「はい、大丈夫です」の二語、それを11時間見つめている。
守れない期限への三つの部分からなる返事と、実際どれくらいかかるかを見積もる簡単な方法を紹介します。
points_ja: ウォータールーの卒論の学生は33.9日と予想して55.5日かかり、最善の予想までに終わったのは29.7%（ビューラー、グリフィン、ロス、学生37人）
自分の見積もりは、壊れるフィルターを入れ忘れる。経験した人に聞く
何をいつまでにできるか、何が動く必要があるか、何が一番大事か
ダニエルはオデットに2週間と言ったが、前回は5週間、今回は34日かかった
東京の「検討します」とシアトルの「問題ないです！」は、どちらも確認前にはいと言っている
episodes.summary_ja: マークさんが、月曜の東京時間朝9時までに、リージョン3のビューがほしいと言います。3日ぶんの仕事で、セナの下書きは「はい、大丈夫です」の二語。ケンタさん（リージョン2は4日と、フィルター修正にもう1日）とリョウさん（大阪のスクリプトは2日のはずが6日）に聞いてから、加藤さんに返事を見せます。火曜朝9時までに1ページのプレビュー、または水曜のあとに完全なビュー、そして「水曜にはどちらが役に立ちますか？」。マークさんは4秒で返します。「あっ。1ページ！！」ダニエルは、ビューラー、グリフィン、ロスの1994年の計画錯誤の研究を紹介します。ウォータールー大学の心理学の学生37人は、卒業論文を33.9日で仕上げると予想し、実際は55.5日。最善の予想までに終わったのは29.7%、楽観的な日までは10.8%でした。限界は、学生、一つの大きなプロジェクト、1994年、他人の作業を見積もる観察者は長く見積もりすぎたこと。言えるのは、自分の予想が一番、壊れるフィルターを入れ忘れやすい、ということだけです。失敗談は、前回5週間かかったデータのエクスポートを、オデットに2週間と言ってしまい、34日かかって、彼女がすでにVPに伝えていたこと。日本とアメリカでは、加藤さんの「検討します」（丁寧な断りが、はいと聞こえる）と「なんとかします」（コストの隠れたはい）と、ローラさんの「本当の期限はいつ？火曜日になったら何が起きる？」、そしてシアトルの明るい「問題ないです！」を比べます。スキルは、代案を添えて押し返すこと（何をいつまでにできるか、何が動くか、何が大事か）。前回のチャレンジの振り返りと、今日のチャレンジ、最後は、ローラさんの水曜に向けた三つの質問で、最後の一つは誰にも答えられず、「推測はしないでください」という引きです。
episodes.practice_ja: 期限にはいと言う前に、前回の似たことが実際どれくらいかかったかを調べる。それから、いつまでに何ができるかで答えて、何が一番大事かを聞く。
